story_text.value:
Hi HN!

profiler-md is a CLI and JS library that converts performance profiles to Markdown across 17 formats (e.g. pprof), 29 profilers (e.g. py-spy), 22 languages (e.g. Rust), and 4 profile types (call stack profiles, call graphs, heap snapshots, and traces).

Earlier this year I tried using AI agents for performance optimization. They weren't very effective because they frequently:

- Speculated about why something was slow from just reading the code

- Made changes, measured the wall time before vs after, and struggled to distinguish real improvements from noise

- Analyzed raw profiles using one-off scripts, which were often subtly incorrect

The issue was that the agents couldn't read a flamegraph like I could. In a flamegraph, I could see what was slow, and when I made changes, I could see whether the targeted work was eliminated. The agents needed a feedback loop like that.

So I wrote a small converter from Node CPU profiles to Markdown. The agents were much more effective when using it, and I realized I also liked reading the Markdown myself!

I felt this had potential, and I use many different programming languages at work, so I decided to build profiler-md. I also wrote an agent skill [1], which I've successfully used to optimize profiler-md itself and its pprof-format dependency (a 78x speedup on a large pprof file [2] and a 3.3x speedup more broadly [3]).

I got to solve some fun problems for this project:

- Making it so that adding a new format, profiler, or profile type is as simple as implementing an interface and adding to a registry. I also have project skills for this!

- Resolving weirdly differing profiler semantics (e.g. around what line numbers mean [4] [5] [6] [7]) by setting up the right interface boundaries.

- Matching functions across profiles for the Markdown diff output. A profile doesn't contain the full code, so this required some heuristics. I evaluated the algorithm by measuring recall (99.9%) and precision (99.7%) on diffs from real version upgrades.

- Designing a call tree renderer that maximizes metrics such as how many of the hottest functions it shows and how much of the profile's self value it covers [8].

I'd love to hear what you think. Try it out and let me know if you have any feedback or questions!

Full disclosure: I work at Anthropic, but this personal project is unrelated to my employer.

[1] https://github.com/TomerAberbach/profiler-md/#skill

[2] https://github.com/DataDog/pprof-format/pull/77

[3] https://github.com/DataDog/pprof-format/pull/107

[4] https://github.com/rbspy/rbspy/issues/409

[5] https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/29240

[6] https://github.com/google/pprof-nodejs/issues/361

[7] https://github.com/NixOS/nix/blob/16fa212a96192479593620e9b9...

[8] https://github.com/TomerAberbach/profiler-md/blob/a1ee95e4b5...

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I made Pizza, an open-source, event-driven AI agent. No `while true`.

Each turn is a state machine. Conversations and tool calls go into an immutable SQLite log. The UI, model context, and session tree are built from that log.

The model gets one tool: a CLI. Reading files, editing code, and running commands all go through it.

You can keep a conversation going without manually starting new sessions. Pizza compacts context as needed, and you can branch from any earlier message.

Agents in separate workspaces talk through `tell`, each doing the work in its own project. An SSH host can be a workspace too: Pizza deploys itself there and runs remotely.

Desktop and terminal interfaces are included. Bring your own model.

https://github.com/pizza-agent/pizza

story_text.value:
Hi, I made a tiny app that lets you turn off the MacBook screen when you work on external monitors.

It does NOT just dim the brightness to zero, the screen is actually turned off via the Apple hardware API, the according desktop is removed, so you have a clean "one big monitor" setup.

- Safe fallback if you turn off the external monitor(s), unplug the monitor cable(s), the app crashes or anything else happens. - Keyboard, touchpad and TouchID still work fine. - Automatic restart. 2 Megabyte size. - Totally niche, I know, but it helps me to concentrate.

The app is commercial ($9 once), but everybody who DMs me here gets a *FREE* lifetime license, and everybody who uses in the feedback form (to report if the apps works on your setup) gets a free lifetime license too.

Thanks ;)

Feel free to try it from the releases or you can install directly via:

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Balázs, and I wanted to share my passion project that I've been building in my free time. It is free, it is open-source, and I've poured a lot of love into making it delightful.

I've spent a lot of time dabbling with agentic ADEs and IDEs since the days of the early VSCode forks. I've switched IDEs more times than I can count. Cursor. Copilot. Codex. PearAI. Orca. Claude Code. OpenCode. Superset. Agent Orchestrator. Windsurf, and then Devin. OpenChamber. Kilo. IntelliJ and VSCode plugins.

This September, I felt sort of stranded. I kept switching tools, losing all my chats, losing time, and frankly, losing love for the very thing that has been getting me out of bed every morning for the past decade. Programming. Building. Tinkering. I've spent more time fighting my tools, being forced back into terminals, being rug-pulled by labs, or being forced into the cloud, when really, I just want to work on my machine.

It was then that I started to jot down my frustrations in a blog post. Not that anyone would read it, especially these days, but my frustrations, I felt, needed an outlet. As I was writing the post, I sort of realised: for the longest time, I'd been observing and obsessing over products like Linear. Raycast. Arc. Their level of detail. Their thoughtful approach to UX. Their grassroots, scratch-a-boring-itch story.

So I decided to scratch my itch, and build an IDE that would stay out of your way. It's called Althar. Delightful to use, calm, and open, rethinking the old paradigms that are holding most of the industry captive. There's no sidebar. There's no built-in text editor. There are no chats (in a traditional sense).

Agents forgetting my project between tasks always annoyed me. So did my overarching goals and milestones getting lost between chats, and agents having no way to coordinate work with one another. In most tools I've tried, they work in silos.

So, in Althar, you organise your work in projects. A project can be a single repository, or many. On top of it sits your project manager, called the coordinator. You talk to her like you would talk to any PM on a project. You could say something like, "Help me make my website responsive and accessible. Also, help me measure the performance with Lighthouse." She will then split the work into three separate tasks, brief individual task agents called leads, assign each task a reviewer agent (we love a second opinion, but it's optional), and send them on their way.

Finished work comes back to you with screenshots, test evidence, and the reviewer's findings settled.

You see everything that's happening on a kanban-like board (though it is NOT kanban), and you're only pulled in when you're actually needed. No need to anxiously watch over terminals and in-flight agent thinking trails.

You can use all of your existing subscriptions. Claude. Codex. OpenCode and so on. It connects to your issue trackers and git hosts, wherever they may be.

Work happens locally. Next week, I hope to add support for remote runners, and I'm also working on a mobile companion.

I hope you'll enjoy it. There is so much to say, so many little details. But it's also early days, so please, if you do find issues, let me know :) Or open a pull request. The open source community has given me so much over the years. It is the best thing about software engineering, and something unique to our profession. I'm excited that I get to give back.

story_text.value:
Hello HN, just wanted to share my project that I've been working on the past months, where I noticed the issue that now we ship faster than setting up the requirements for the project. So I thought of building secureVibe to find vulnerabilities in your codebase.

Now I have a MVP where it doesn't just scan the code and show random analysis I used Tree-sitter and AST to understand code context to validate vulnerabilities found as it builds a graph of application routes, handlers and database calls so it helps to determine whether findings are confirmed or likely.

Briefly the features: 1- shows all vulnerabilities in your code with code snippets

2-fixing with ai option (optional with your own api key for now)

3- ask the graph feature as you can ask where the attacker can exploit my website or authentication issues (I used graphify as foundation for it )

4- You can filter vulnerabilities categories (like Cwe, database injection and more) from dashboard and you can download it as html report simple interactive one so you can fix it on your own later.

I would love to know your thoughts and feedback to continue on the development on it like some of the problems I faced is benchmarks to validate security rules. With some research I found openssf benchmark

On the OpenSSF CVE benchmark, the raw F1 score was 77.5, but still I face some issues with false positive

so would really appreciate feedback to continue on developing with next phases.

Even though with these issues Its still working well, it is efficient and fast and preferably start with TypeScript repos first for it.

story_text.value:
I originally built this visualisation of the GCAT (https://planet4589.org/space/gcat/) database a few years ago as part of some university coursework. It then sat collecting dust for a while, but I've finally found the time to give it a bit of a visual overhaul. It's now something I'm happy to share.

The main motivation with creating this was to show two things: just how much stuff is currently orbiting Earth, and how dramatically that number has increased over the last few years.

Speaking to some friends about this, we agreed that it's easy to read statistics about how many satellites there are, but it's hard to put those numbers into perspective. Visualising this from space and seeing everything orbiting our planet at once really drives home the scale of it!

title.value: Show HN: Every Satellite in Orbit Since 1957

The main motivation with creating this was to show two things: just how much stuff is currently orbiting Earth, and how dramatically that number has increased over the last few years.

Speaking to some friends about this, we agreed that it's easy to read statistics about how many satellites there are, but it's hard to put those numbers into perspective. Visualising this from space and seeing everything orbiting our planet at once really drives home the scale of it!
